record.paper_title: Statements and open problems on decidable sets X ⊆ N that contain informal notions and refer to the current knowledge on X
record.original_question: Does there exist a decidable set X ⊆ N such that Condition (2), Condition (4), and Condition (5) hold, but both Condition (1) and Condition (3) fail? That is, can one find a naturally defined set X with decidable membership and many known elements, conjectured but not proved to be infinite, for which there is no known threshold integer of the type in Condition (1), and for which a known algorithm with no input does return the truth value of the statement that X is infinite?

evidence.quote:
Open Problem 3. Is there a set X ⊆ N that satisfies the conjunction
¬(Condition 1) ∧ (Condition 2) ∧ ¬(Condition 3) ∧ (Condition 4) ∧ (Condition 5)?

Definition 1.2. Conditions (1)-(5) concern sets X ⊆ N.
(1) A known algorithm with no input returns an integer n satisfying card(X) < ω ⇒ X ⊆ (−∞, n].
(2) A known algorithm for every k ∈ N decides whether or not k ∈ X.
(3) No known algorithm with no input returns the logical value of the statement card(X) = ω.
(4) There are many elements of X and it is conjectured, though so far unproven, that X is infinite.
(5) X is naturally defined. The infiniteness is false or unproven. X has the simplest definition among known sets Y ⊆ N with the same set of known elements.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider subsets $X \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ (where $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$) and the following five conditions:

(1) There exists a known algorithm that takes no input and returns an integer $n$ such that, if $X$ is finite, then $X \subseteq (-\infty, n]$ (i.e., a known threshold bounding $X$ in the finite case).

(2) There exists a known algorithm that, for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, decides whether or not $k \in X$ (i.e., $X$ is decidable, with an explicitly known decision procedure).

(3) No known algorithm with no input returns the truth value of the statement "$\operatorname{card}(X) = \omega$" (i.e., the infiniteness of $X$ is not algorithmically known).

(4) Many elements of $X$ are known, and it is conjectured—though so far unproven—that $X$ is infinite.

(5) $X$ is naturally defined; the assertion that $X$ is infinite is either false or unproven; and $X$ has the simplest definition among known sets $Y \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that share the same set of currently known elements.

Question: Does there exist a set $X \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that
$$\neg(\text{Condition 1}) \;\wedge\; (\text{Condition 2}) \;\wedge\; \neg(\text{Condition 3}) \;\wedge\; (\text{Condition 4}) \;\wedge\; (\text{Condition 5})$$
holds? Equivalently: can one exhibit a naturally defined decidable set $X \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ with many known elements, conjectured but not proved to be infinite, for which no known algorithm produces an integer threshold of the type in Condition (1), yet a known algorithm with no input does return the truth value of "$X$ is infinite"?
